options.text: Ability to form and sustain relationships

questions.explanation:

questions.question_text: Unconditional positive regard is a feature of
questions.explanation:
Carl Rogers developed client-centered psychotherapy, in which therapists attempt to produce an atmosphere where clients can reconstruct their strivings for self-actualisation. Therapists hold clients in unconditional positive regard, which is non-judgemental acceptance. Other therapeutic practices include attention to the present, focus on clients' feelings, emphasis on process, trust in the potential and self-responsibility of clients, and a philosophy grounded in a positive attitude towards clients, rather than a preconceived structure of treatment.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1088.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies uses 'mindfulness' as a therapeutic strategy?
questions.explanation:
Dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) was introduced in 1991 by Linehan and colleagues as a treatment for borderline personality disorder (BPD). Patients with BPD are supported in understanding their own emotional experiences and are taught new skills for dealing with their distress through a combination of group and individual therapy sessions. DBT is a complex treatment combining CBT interventions with Eastern meditative practice, notably mindfulness.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 916-917.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a self-rated scale?
questions.explanation:
The Beck depression inventory is a self-rated questionnaire that contains 21 statements, with four possible responses for each. A total score of >17 indicates moderate depression and >30 indicates severe depression.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 97.

questions.question_text: In the management of chronic fatigue syndrome, dividing symptom-producing activities into smaller parts with interspersed rest intervals is referred to as
questions.explanation:
In the management of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), medical providers can teach patients how to recognise their own personal energy limits and use 'pacing' (dividing symptom-producing activities into smaller parts with interspersed rest intervals) to stay within these limits. Once pacing is effectively used, some patients may be able to increase available energy and functioning, while avoiding post-exertional worsening. Of note, though CBT and graded exercise therapy (GET) have been previously recommended for CFS, the trials have been widely criticized for several design issues. Many patients have since reported that CBT and GET have not only fallen short of delivering significant improvements but have also led to worsened healthy due to ill-advised activity and exercise prescriptions.
Ref: Friedberg F et al. Rethinking the Standard of Care for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome. Journal of general internal medicine. 2020 Mar;35(3):906-9.

questions.question_text: Defence mechanisms are a function of the
questions.explanation:
Defence mechanisms are a function of the ego. At each phase of libidinal development, specific drive components evoke characteristic ego defences. Defences can be grouped hierarchically according to the relative degree of maturity associated with them. Mental disorder can be characterised by the persistence of primitive defence mechanisms, with immature defences seen in early childhood, mental illnesses, and personality disturbances. Neurotic defences are seen in older children or adults experiencing stress or anxiety. Mature defences are seen in functioning adults.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1065.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 891.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a process of cognitive therapy?
questions.explanation:
The cognitive therapy approach includes four processes: eliciting automatic thoughts, testing automatic thoughts, identifying maladaptive underlying assumptions, and testing the validity of maladaptive assumptions.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 768.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a behavioural technique used in CBT?
questions.explanation:
Among the behavioural techniques in CBT are scheduling activities, mastery and pleasure, graded task assignments, cognitive rehearsal, self-reliance training, role playing, and diversion techniques. To simplify situations and allow for mini-accomplishments, therapists often break tasks into subtasks, as in graded task assignments, to show patients that they can succeed.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 770-771.

questions.question_text: Corrective recapitulation of the primary family group is one of the therapeutic factors described in
questions.explanation:
Yalom described a set of therapeutic factors common to many types of groups. These include the instillation of hope, universality, imparting information, altruism, corrective familial experience (or corrective recapitulation of the primary family group), development of socialisation techniques, imitation of adaptive behaviour, interpersonal learning, group cohesion, catharsis, and existential factors. In corrective familial experience, the group recreates the family of origin for some members who can work through conflicts psychologically through group interaction (e.g., sibling rivalry, anger toward parents).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 904.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022.  . 757.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered to be the most important factor related to positive therapeutic effects in group therapy?
questions.explanation:
In group therapy, cohesion is the sense that the group is working together toward a common goal. It is also referred to as a sense of 'we-ness'. Cohesion is believed to be the most important factor related to positive therapeutic effects.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 757.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true regarding the Camberwell Family Interview (CFI)?

options.text: The CFI has shown poor predictive validity
The CFI provides data on ten domains
It is a gold standard assessment of activities of daily living
It was originally designed to be conducted with families of patients with schizophrenia

correct_answer.text: It was originally designed to be conducted with families of patients with schizophrenia

correct_answers.text: It was originally designed to be conducted with families of patients with schizophrenia

questions.explanation:
The Camberwell Family Interview (CFI) is a semi-structured interview that is considered the gold standard measure of expressed emotion in families of individuals with mental health problems. Originally designed for patients with schizophrenia, the CFI is conducted with key family members and focuses on the impact of the patient’s condition on the daily life of the family. High expressed emotion (EE) in families is a significant predictor of symptomatic relapse and other negative outcomes. The CFI is administered without the patient being present and is recorded so that it can later be coded. It does not include structured questions, but only a guidance for eliciting information from the caregiver about the patient’s symptoms in the period before relapse or re‑hospitalization. The interview is audio-recorded and later coded. The CFI has shown considerable concurrent and predictive validity and provides data on five domains of EE: Critical Comments, Emotional Over-involvement, Hostility, Warmth, and Positive Remarks.
Ref: Dodd, C.G., Schoonover, C.E. Camberwell Interview for Assessing Expressed Emotion in Families. In: Lebow, J., Chambers, A., Breunlin, D. (eds) Encyclopedia of Couple and Family Therapy. 2018. pp. 1-4.
O'Driscoll C et al. Caregiving processes and expressed emotion in psychosis, a cross-cultural, meta-analytic review. Schizophrenia Research. 2019 Jun 1;208:8-15.

Motivational interviewing (MI) is a technique used to motivate the patient to change maladaptive behaviour. The therapist relies on empathy to convey understanding, provides support by noting the patient's strengths, and explores the ambivalence and conflicting thoughts or feelings that the patient may have about change. Principles of MI include expressing empathy, developing discrepancy, rolling with resistance, and supporting self-efficacy and optimism. questions.explanation:
Jean Piaget's contributions to the understanding of cognitive development has had significant influence in developmental psychology and major implications for interventions with children, both educational and clinical. He created a broad theoretical system for the development of cognitive abilities and was widely renowned as a developmental psychologist. According to Piaget, there are four major stages that lead to the capacity for adult thought: sensorimotor, preoperational thought, concrete operations, and formal operations.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1007.

questions.question_text: Interpersonal psychotherapy is characterised by all of the following except

options.text: 12 to 16 hourly sessions, usually occurring weekly

questions.explanation:
Interpersonal therapy (IPT) was developed in the 1970s by Klerman and Weissman as a treatment for depressive illness, and later developed for use in other disorders. IPT is a practical, short-term therapy (12-16 hour-long sessions) that aims, by improving interpersonal functioning, to improve emotional symptoms. Illnesses are viewed as medical disorders, diagnosed according to standard criteria, and rated in severity by rating scales. A key feature of IPT involves ‘giving the sick role’ to the patient. The initial phase of treatment includes the establishment of the ‘sick role’ and completion of an interpersonal inventory (description of current relationships).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 914-915.

questions.question_text: Which of the following behavioural treatments is useful in trichotillomania?
questions.explanation:
Habit reversal training (HRT) is a set of cognitive behavioural techniques that have been shown efficacious in the treatment of childhood and adult trichotillomania (hair pulling disorder). Components of HRT include awareness training, competing for response training, and social support. Also, therapists use stimulus control to change the patient's environment so that hairpulling is more effortful or less reinforcing.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. р. 425.

questions.question_text: Psychodynamic psychotherapy can be used for a wide variety of disorders, but it is contraindicated for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Psychodynamic psychotherapy is generally contraindicated in acute psychosis due to increasing expressed emotion and the inherent neuropsychological deficits associated with this mental state. It is also contraindicated in severe depressive illness (because of psychomotor retardation), dementia/delirium (where treatment of organic pathology is first line), and in some individuals where there is acute suicide risk.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 884, 903.

questions.question_text: Which of the following techniques is considered to be anti-therapeutic in group therapy?
questions.explanation: Scape goating, idealization of the therapist and coupling are considered to be anti-therapeutic in group therapy. Scapegoating is an explanation of discrimination based on the idea of frustration-aggression. The work of Bion, Ezriel and Foulkes were crucial in the development of group therapy.

questions.question_text: The basis of object relations theory is that the primary motivational drive of an individual is to seek
questions.explanation:
In the mid-twentieth century, Winnicott, Klein, Fairbairn, and others developed object relations theory, which emphasises the importance of relationships - rather than drives such as sexuality and aggression - in affecting the mind. The theory describes a model of infant psychological development, links abnormal early experiences to symptoms in later life, and uses this as a basis for interpretation in therapy. Object relations theory remains significant in modern psychoanalytic practice.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 896.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not included in Bion's basic assumptions?
questions.explanation:
Wilfred Bion’s ‘basic assumptions’ describe three ways in which groups may function: dependency, fight-flight, or pairing. He moved away from emphasising the content of patients’ narratives to thinking about how we structure the world around us through our thinking and how this, in turn, allows our internal worlds to develop.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 888.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most often seen in the process of supportive psychotherapy?

options.text: Good psychological mindedness in the patient
Patient seeking exploration of cause of symptoms

questions.explanation:
Supportive psychotherapy aims at the creation of a therapeutic relationship as a temporary buttress for the deficient patient. It is generally indicated for those who have poor ego strength and whose potential for decompensation is high. Amenable patients include those in acute crisis and unable to cope; patients with chronic severe pathology and fragile or deficient ego functioning; patients whose cognitive deficits and physical symptoms make them particularly unsuitable for an insight-oriented approach; and individuals who are psychologically unmotivated. The relationship between therapist and patient allows a therapist to display behaviour different from the destructive or unproductive behaviour of a patient's parent. If the parent had overly authoritarian parents, the therapist's friendly, flexible, nonjudgemental, nonauthoritarian - but at times firm and limit-setting - attitude allows the patient to adjust to, be led by, and identify with a new parent figure.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 751-752.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is most associated with a good response to psychodynamic psychotherapy?

options.text: Positive perception of the therapist throughout treatment
Motivation developed after sustained effort from therapist
Patient can understand issues in psychological terms

correct_answer.text: Patient can understand issues in psychological terms

correct_answers.text: Patient can understand issues in psychological terms

questions.explanation:
To benefit from psychodynamic psychotherapy, patients should be highly motivated, able to tolerate frustration and anxiety, have good impulse control, be able to form meaningful relationships, and be capable of insight and abstract thought. 'Psychological mindedness' refers to the capacity for insight and to understand problems in psychological terms. If this is lacking, a supportive method may be preferred over an exploratory method like psychodynamic psychotherapy.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 882-884.

questions.question_text: Genetic counselling is classified under which type of counselling?
questions.explanation:
Risk counselling is used to guide an informed decision (e.g. prenatal interventions, genetic counselling). Risk counselling is differentiated from other forms of counselling by the fact that the counsellor is clearly 'the expert' and has access to specialist information. Nonetheless, the basic goal of enabling the patient to come to their own decision, with appropriate information and support, remains the same.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 923.

questions.question_text: Idealization and denigration are products of which of the following Kleinian processes?
questions.explanation:
Through her study of early life and children's play, Melanie Klein proposed that aggressive and destructive forces were central components of early development.
• Paranoid-schizoid position: infants' mode of organising experience in which all aspects of infant and mother are split into good and bad elements (idealized or denigrated)
• Depressive position: once able to integrate good and bad, infants become concerned that they may have harmed or destroyed the mother through hostile and sadistic fantasies; the mother is viewed ambivalently as having both positive and negative aspects, and as the target of a mixture of loving and hateful feelings
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1083.

questions.question_text: Which of the following group therapies has a high level of leader input?

options.text: Structured groups for drug or alcohol use

correct_answer.text: Structured groups for drug or alcohol use

correct_answers.text: Structured groups for drug or alcohol use

questions.explanation: Group therapies can be classified according to the objectives of the group and how the group is led or managed (leadership). Highly specific target oriented groups include structured groups for drug use or alcohol use, activity groups like occupational therapy, groups etc. These groups have high level of leader input. Psychodrama, music therapy, systems centred groups are some less specific therapies but are highly directed by the leader or therapist. Problem solving therapy and psycho educational groups are highly specific but have low level of therapist activity. Support groups, art therapy, interpersonal therapy and groups like Tavistock model analytic groups have low level of leader activity and have low specificity with respect to treatment goals

questions.question_text: A definite termination date is set at beginning of treatment in which of the following therapies?
questions.explanation:
Brief focal psychotherapy (Tavistock-Malan) is a type of brief psychodynamic psychotherapy. It was originally developed in the 1950s by the Balint team at the Tavistock Clinic in London. Malan, a member of the team, reported the results of the therapy. In Malan's routine, therapists identify the transference early and interpret it and the negative transference. Therapists formulate a circumscribed focus and set a termination date in advance, and patients work through grief and anger about termination.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 752-753.

questions.question_text: Which of the following therapies uses techniques such as circular questioning and hypothesising?
questions.explanation:
Milan systemic family therapy was developed in the early 1970s in response to the closure of large psychiatric institutions in Italy. It introduced the concepts of ‘reframing’ the problem and hypothesizing, as well as ideas about neutrality and curiosity, with the therapist taking more of a ‘not-knowing’, non-expert stance. There is an emphasis on circular and reflexive questioning. In a circular fashion, each family member comments and reflects on each other’s response.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 719.
Barbetta P. Milan Systemic Family Therapy. In: Lebow J.L., Chambers A.L., Breunlin D.C. (eds) Encyclopedia of Couple and Family Therapy. 2019.

questions.question_text: Thought stopping is a behavioural technique commonly used in the treatment of
questions.explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is recommended by NICE for the management of OCD, but essentially takes a behavioural approach. This includes response prevention (useful in ritualistic behaviour), thought stopping (helpful in ruminations), and exposure techniques (for obsessions).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 386.

questions.explanation:

Aim to improve function
Break cycle of reassurance and repeat presentations
Behavioural therapy: response prevention and exposure to illness cues

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the stance that is held by the therapist while administering interpersonal psychotherapy?
questions.explanation:
The interpersonal therapist is an active advocate and facilitator to encourage the patient to see their problems from different perspectives, to make attempts at change, and to return to discuss their successes and failures at subsequent sessions.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 915.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not one of the therapeutic techniques used in interpersonal therapy?
questions.explanation:
Techniques in IPT include facilitation of the grieving process; mourning the loss of the old role and learning to embrace the challenges of the new role (in role transition focus); teaching of specific communication, problem solving, or conflict resolution skills; and role play.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 915.

questions.question_text: Systematic desensitisation involves all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) is frequently used in the treatment of phobic anxiety disorders. It is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). Three steps involve: 1) Relaxation training, 2) Constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and 3) Desensitisation of the stimulus. The patient is exposed to a graded hierarchy of anxiety-provoking situations in a stepwise fashion while being taught to practice the relaxation techniques (e.g. a young woman with a spider phobia is taught relaxation techniques and then exposed to experiences starting from the lowest level of her hierarchy of anxieties - such as going to the cellar where there is the potential to come across a spider - then progressively going up the ladder to the highest - such as handling a spider).
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT part of Beck's theory of depression?
questions.explanation:
According to cognitive theory developed by Aaron Beck, depression results from cognitive distortions present in people susceptible to depression. Elements of cognitive theory include the cognitive triad, schema, cognitive distortions, arbitrary inference, specific/selective abstraction, overgeneralisation, magnification & minimisation, personalisation, and absolutist, dichotomous thinking.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 399.

questions.question_text: Who described the unconscious as composed of both the collective unconscious and personal unconscious?
questions.explanation:
Carl Jung expanded on Freud's concept of the unconscious by describing the collective unconscious as consisting of all humankind's common, shared mythological and symbolic past. The collective unconscious includes archetypes (representational images and configurations with universal symbolic meanings). The personal unconscious is an individual's unconscious, comprising complexes (sets of ideas and feelings triggered by interpersonal interactions).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1082.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 888.

questions.question_text: Strategic family therapy is o!ered to a struggling family. Which of the following techniques is used in this therapy?
questions.explanation:
In the model of strategic family therapy, developed by Haley, problems always arise because of di#culties with hierarchy within the family system. Haley suggested that rather than attempting to resolve this, the family is ambivalent about having the problem, as it provides some gain for them. The therapist takes a more strategic stance to overcome their resistance, such as using ‘paradox’ and setting family tasks such as ‘prescribing’ or ‘pretending’ the problematic symptom.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 718.

questions.question_text: The 'repressive barrier' to censor unacceptable wishes and desires is maintained by the
questions.explanation:
The preconscious contains those ideas and memories that are capable of entering the conscious mind. The preconscious performs a 'censorship' function by examining these ideas and memories and sending those which are unacceptable back to the unconscious (maintains the 'repressive barrier').
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 890.

questions.question_text: Which type of group psychotherapy is indicated for the treatment of phobias?
questions.explanation:
Indications for behavioural group therapy include phobias and anxiety disorders.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 756.

questions.question_text: Childhood experience and exploration of the unconscious mind is the focus of which of the following forms of therapy?
questions.explanation:
Therapies that conceptualise an unconscious mind affecting our perceptions and actions can be considered part of the school of dynamic psychotherapies. Traumatic experiences, particularly those in early life/childhood, give rise to psychological conflict. The greater part of mental activity is unconscious, and conscious mind is protected from the experiences of this conflict by in-built defences, designed to decrease 'unpleasure' and to diminish anxiety.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 898-902.

questions.question_text: The first step in the assessment of someone presenting with fear of spiders is
questions.explanation:
Goals of assessment for psychotherapy:
Understanding what the patient expects (or wants) from therapy
Obtaining a careful history/narrative of the problem
Establishing whether the patient can form a therapeutic relationship and make use of therapy
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 884.

questions.question_text: Which type of family therapy emphasises clearly defined boundaries between the parents and children?
questions.explanation:
Minuchin proposed that clear rules govern optimal family organisation and structure, with a focus on hierarchy, subsystems, and boundaries. Challenges to this structure results in problems. The structural family therapist takes a directive, 'expert' stance to change family behaviours and re-establish the preferred structure.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 718.

questions.question_text: During a psychotherapy session a patient states that he has been 'abusing' his children, but then quickly changes the topic. What should be done next?

options.text: Maintain boundaries and end the session as planned
Terminate the interview immediately and inform social services
Tell him that you will inform the concerned authority
Ignore this and continue with the flow of the patient's speech

questions.explanation:
Be alert to the possibility of abuse and respond to the patient's concern. Get as much information as possible.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 718.

questions.question_text: Which of the following should not be present in a patient about to start psychotherapy?
questions.explanation:
Important psychological factors in patients appropriate for psychotherapy include psychological mindedness, motivation for insight and change, adequate ego strength and reality testing, the ability to form and maintain relationships, and the ability to tolerate change and frustration. Psychotherapy is generally contraindicated in acute psychosis due to increasing expressed emotion and the inherent neuropsychological deficits associated with this mental state.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 884-885.

questions.question_text: In psychotherapy, the term 'psychological mindedness' refers to which of the following?

options.text: Ability to form a therapeutic alliance
Ability to understand problems in physical terms
Ability to understand problems in psychological terms

correct_answer.text: Ability to understand problems in psychological terms

correct_answers.text: Ability to understand problems in psychological terms

questions.explanation:
‘Psychological mindedness’ refers to the capacity for insight and to understand problems in psychological terms (i.e. ‘can the patient think about their thoughts?’). If this is lacking, a supportive method may be preferred.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 884.

questions.question_text: Of the following, a desired cognitive outcome when treating someone with hypochondriasis is

options.text: The complete absence of thoughts of illness
Avoidance of seeking medical help when symptoms are troublesome
Less distress at thoughts of illness

correct_answer.text: Less distress at thoughts of illness

correct_answers.text: Less distress at thoughts of illness

questions.explanation:
Psychotherapeutic management of hypochondriasis: Psychotherapeutic management of hypochondriasis:
Aim to improve function
Break cycle Break cycle of reassurance of reassurance and repeat presentations
Behavioural therapy: Behavioural therapy: response prevention and exposure to illness cues
CBT: identify and challenge misinterpretations, substitution of realistic interpretation, graded exposure to illness-related situations, modification of core illness beliefs
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 871.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not a component of CBT for delusions in psychosis?

options.text: Decreasing the impact of positive symptoms
Providing alternate explanations to unusual experiences

questions.explanation: Though CBT is gaining popularity in treating psychotic symptoms, often, clinicians are unsure about the symptoms targeted in CBT. According to Birchwood, the target is the emotional dysfunction that accompanies psychotic experience and not the psychotic symptoms per se. Turkington described the following elements in CBT for psychosis: Therapeutic alliance, Improving medication adherence, Providing alternate explanations to unusual experiences e.g. normalisation, Decreasing the impact of positive symptoms e.g. addressing the omnipotence of voices and Graded reality testing using peripheral questioning and inference chaining.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes Bion's principle of 'containing?

options.text: A baby holds on to its emotions in so that it does not upset the mother
The therapist holds a patient's inner experience and returns it in a modified form
The therapist practices restraint and doesn't have any feelings
The patient holds on to their feelings and doesn't let them out
A mother holds in her emotions so that she does not upset her baby

correct_answer.text: The therapist holds a patient's inner experience and returns it in a modified form

correct_answers.text: The therapist holds a patient's inner experience and returns it in a modified form

questions.explanation:
Wilfred Bion developed the notion that the therapist must contain what the patient has projected so that it is processed and returned to the patient in a modified form. Bion believed that a similar process occurs between mother and infant. Bion described the mother as a container that provides the baby an emotional presence without words, through attention to the baby who is unable to express itself in words. The mother perceives signals from the baby, picks up the messages, and names them. In a provider-patient relationship, the provider may translate the patient's pain, fear, and distress into words and provide the patient with hope for a good future where the patient may develop resilience, cope with the pain, and manage the illness. The provider can hold the unbearable inner experience of the patient until the patient can deal with the emotions evoked.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1080.
Gabay G, Ben-Asher S. An Inverted Container in Containing and Not Containing Hospitalized Patients-A Multidisciplinary Narrative Inquiry. Frontiers in Public Health. 2022;10.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a correct description of transference?

options.text: Good eye contact throughout the therapy session
The patient's response to the therapist based on previous relationships
The therapist's response to the patient based on previous relationships

correct_answer.text: The patient's response to the therapist based on previous relationships

correct_answers.text: The patient's response to the therapist based on previous relationships

questions.explanation:
Transference is the unconscious development, in the patient, of feelings, thoughts, attitudes, and patterns of behaviour towards the therapist that recapitulate earlier life relationships, most usually the patient’s relationships with their parents. Transference is viewed as a defence against the reality of relationships with others.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 890.

questions.question_text: A psychotherapist notices that she feels bored in the presence of one particular patient. She has repeatedly cancelled appointments with him. This is most likely due to
questions.explanation:
Countertransference is the process in which the therapist unconsciously displaces onto the patient patterns of behaviour or emotional reactions as if the patient were a significant figure from earlier in the therapist’s life. Therapists should be alert to signs of countertransference issues (missed appointments by the therapist, boredom, or sleepiness in a session).
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 3.

questions.question_text: All of the following are described by Yalom as group curative factors, except
questions.explanation:
Yalom described a set of therapeutic factors common to many types of groups. These include the instillation of hope, universality, imparting information, altruism, corrective familial experience (or corrective recapitulation of the primary family group), development of socialisation techniques, imitation of adaptive behaviour, interpersonal learning, group cohesion, catharsis, and existential factors.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 904.
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 757.

questions.question_text: Which of the following theories best suits the explanation for someone with a borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
Melanie Klein viewed projection and introjection as the primary defensive operations in the first months of life. Infants project derivatives of the death instinct into the mother and then fear attack from the 'bad mother', a phenomenon that Klein referred to as persecutory anxiety. This anxiety is intimately associated with the paranoid-schizoid position, infants' mode of organising experience in which all aspects of infant and mother are split into good and bad elements. People with borderline personalities are seen as displaying primitive defence mechanisms such as splitting and projective identification.
Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 1083.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 526.

questions.question_text: Your colleague asks you what has been shown to predict a good response to psychotherapy for depression. Your response will be

options.text: Lack of prior exposure to therapy
The therapist's contribution to therapeutic alliance
The patient's perception of the working alliance with the therapist.

correct_answer.text: The patient's perception of the working alliance with the therapist.

correct_answers.text: The patient's perception of the working alliance with the therapist.

questions.explanation: The relationship between therapeutic alliance and treatment outcome was examined for depressed outpatients who received interpersonal psychotherapy, cognitive-behavior therapy, imipramine with clinical management, or placebo with clinical management in NIMH collaborative trial for depression treatment (Krupnick et al, 2006). Therapeutic alliance was found to have a significant e!ect on clinical outcome for both psychotherapies and for active and placebo pharmacotherapy. Ratings of patient contribution to the alliance were significantly related to treatment outcome; ratings of therapist contribution to the alliance and outcome were not significantly linked. These results indicate that the therapeutic alliance is a common factor with significant influence on outcome ( The role of the therapeutic alliance in psychotherapy and ... (n.d.). Retrieved from [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8698947](https://www.google.com/search?q=http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8698947)). Positive perception of therapist throughout treatment (idealization) is not necessary and may even be counterproductive in some cases.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a crucial step in the psychological treatment of phobias?
questions.explanation:
Systematic desensitisation (Wolpe) is frequently used in the treatment of phobic anxiety disorders. It is based on the behavioural principle of reciprocal inhibition (i.e. anxiety and relaxation cannot coexist). Three steps involve: 1) Relaxation training, 2) Constructing a hierarchy of anxieties, and 3) Desensitisation of the stimulus.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a form of psychodynamic psychotherapy specifically designed and manualised for the treatment of borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
Mentalisation-based therapy (MBT) is a form of psychodynamic psychotherapy specifically designed and manualised for individuals with borderline personality disorder (BPD). The therapy seeks to address disorganised attachment and the individual’s failure to develop mentalizing capacities as a result of early attachment experiences. MBT has been shown in studies to be e!ective in the management of BPD.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 539.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of psychotherapy is suitable in a child with learning di#culties and behavioural dyscontrol?
questions.explanation:
Behaviour therapy can be used to alter maladaptive patterns of behaviour in children with learning di#culties and behavioural dyscontrol.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 908.

questions.question_text: Which of the following modes of therapy has the least empirical evidence for the treatment of borderline personality disorder and is not recommended by NICE?
questions.explanation:
Psychological therapies for the management of borderline personality disorder include transference-focused psychotherapy, mentalisation-based therapy (MBT), dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), cognitive analytic therapy (CAT), CBT, and IPT. Arising from ‘comprehensive distancing’ in the early 1908s, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) developed into its modern form through the late 1980s and 1990s. It is based on functional contextualism and is derived as a clinical application of the relational frame theory, a behavioural account of human thought and cognition. Provisional low-quality evidence has shown ACT may be at least as e!ective in treating anxiety disorders, depression, addiction, and somatic health problems as established psychological interventions. However, further methodologically robust trials are required.
Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the treatment and management of borderline personality disorder. Updated edition 2018.
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. pp. 538-539, 924-925.
